name: Hammurabi
description: Sixth king of the First Babylonian dynasty, who unified much of Mesopotamia and promulgated the Code of Hammurabi — one of the earliest surviving comprehensive legal codes, inscribed on a diorite stele with 282 laws governing commerce, property, family, and justice under the principle of proportional retribution.

name: Ramesses II
description: Third pharaoh of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty, reigning 66 years. Fought the Hittites at Kadesh (c. 1274 BCE), concluding history's earliest surviving peace treaty, and built monumentally at Abu Simbel, Karnak, and the Ramesseum. His mummy survives in Cairo.

name: Confucius
description: Chinese philosopher of the Spring and Autumn period whose teachings on ethics, filial piety, ritual propriety, and good governance — compiled by disciples in the Analects — became the moral and administrative foundation of imperial China for two millennia.

name: Socrates
description: Athenian philosopher who wrote nothing yet reoriented Greek thought toward ethics and epistemology through relentless public questioning — the Socratic method. Tried for impiety and corrupting the youth, he accepted the death sentence by hemlock rather than abandon philosophy.

name: Alexander the Great
description: Macedonian king who conquered the Achaemenid Persian Empire in a decade, campaigning from Greece to the Indus without losing a major battle. His conquests spread Greek language and culture across the Near East, inaugurating the Hellenistic age; he died at 32 in Babylon.

name: Ashoka
description: Third Mauryan emperor of India who, after the bloody conquest of Kalinga, converted to Buddhism and governed by dhamma — moral law — promulgated through rock and pillar edicts across the subcontinent. His patronage transformed Buddhism into a world religion.

name: Qin Shi Huang
description: First emperor of a unified China (221 BCE). Standardized script, currency, weights and axle widths, connected defensive walls into an early Great Wall, and was entombed at Xi'an with the Terracotta Army — thousands of individually modelled clay soldiers.

name: Julius Caesar
description: Roman general and statesman who conquered Gaul, defied the Senate by crossing the Rubicon, won the civil war, and was named dictator perpetuo — precipitating his assassination on the Ides of March and, with it, the fall of the Republic his heir Augustus replaced with the Principate.

name: Cleopatra VII
description: Last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt, a polyglot administrator who allied with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony to preserve Egyptian independence. After defeat at Actium she died by suicide, and Egypt became a Roman province.

name: Augustus
description: First Roman emperor. Caesar's adopted heir defeated Antony and Cleopatra, then converted military supremacy into constitutional disguise — the Principate — inaugurating two centuries of internal stability, the Pax Romana, while rebuilding Rome in marble.

name: Boudica
description: Queen of the Iceni who led a massive British revolt against Roman rule after the annexation of her kingdom, destroying Camulodunum, Londinium, and Verulamium before defeat. She became an enduring symbol of resistance.

name: Constantine I
description: Roman emperor who legalized Christianity with the Edict of Milan (313), convened the Council of Nicaea (325), and founded Constantinople on the Bosporus — decisions that shaped European religion and geopolitics for a millennium.

name: Justinian I
description: Byzantine emperor whose jurists codified Roman law into the Corpus Juris Civilis — the foundation of most modern civil-law systems — while his generals briefly reconquered Italy and North Africa and his architects raised the Hagia Sophia.

name: Charlemagne
description: King of the Franks crowned Emperor of the Romans by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day 800, uniting most of western Europe for the first time since Rome. His court sparked the Carolingian Renaissance of learning, script, and administration.

name: Al-Khwarizmi
description: Persian polymath at Baghdad's House of Wisdom whose treatise on al-jabr gave algebra its name and whose Latinized name gave us 'algorithm'. His works transmitted Hindu-Arabic numerals to Europe.

name: William the Conqueror
description: Duke of Normandy who won the English crown at Hastings in 1066, replacing the Anglo-Saxon elite with Norman lords, commissioning the Domesday survey of his new kingdom, and permanently binding English institutions and language to continental Europe.

name: Saladin
description: Kurdish sultan of Egypt and Syria who united the Muslim Near East, crushed the crusader army at Hattin (1187), and retook Jerusalem — yet won a chivalrous reputation among his Frankish enemies during the Third Crusade against Richard the Lionheart.

name: Genghis Khan
description: Founder of the Mongol Empire, history's largest contiguous land empire. Unified the steppe tribes, revolutionized cavalry warfare and military organization, and opened Eurasia to unprecedented exchange — at catastrophic human cost to conquered populations.

name: Thomas Aquinas
description: Dominican friar whose Summa Theologiae synthesized Aristotelian philosophy with Christian doctrine, defining scholastic method and remaining the touchstone of Catholic theology. Canonized 1323.

name: Mansa Musa
description: Emperor of Mali whose 1324 hajj to Mecca, distributing so much gold that he depressed prices in Cairo for years, advertised West Africa's wealth to the world. He made Timbuktu a centre of Islamic scholarship.

name: Joan of Arc
description: Peasant visionary who convinced the Dauphin to give her an army, lifted the siege of Orléans, and turned the Hundred Years' War toward France before capture, an English-run heresy trial, and burning at nineteen. Rehabilitated 1456; canonized 1920.

name: Johannes Gutenberg
description: Mainz goldsmith who combined movable metal type, oil-based ink, and a screw press into a printing system around 1450. The resulting collapse in the cost of texts — beginning with his 42-line Bible — accelerated the Renaissance, Reformation, and Scientific Revolution.

name: Leonardo da Vinci
description: Florentine painter, engineer, and anatomist — the archetypal Renaissance polymath. Painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper while filling thousands of notebook pages with studies of anatomy, water, flight, and machines centuries ahead of fabrication.

name: Christopher Columbus
description: Genoese navigator whose 1492 Atlantic crossing under Castilian sponsorship opened sustained contact between Eurasia and the Americas — initiating the Columbian Exchange of crops, peoples, and diseases, and the era of European colonization with its devastating consequences for indigenous populations.

name: Martin Luther
description: German friar whose Ninety-five Theses (1517) against indulgences ignited the Protestant Reformation. His doctrine of justification by faith, vernacular Bible translation, and defiance at Worms fractured Latin Christendom permanently.

name: Suleiman the Magnificent
description: Longest-reigning Ottoman sultan, under whom the empire reached its zenith — taking Belgrade, Rhodes, and most of Hungary, besieging Vienna, reforming law (hence 'Kanuni', the Lawgiver), and patronizing a golden age of Ottoman architecture under Sinan.

name: Nicolaus Copernicus
description: Polish canon and astronomer whose De revolutionibus (1543) placed the Sun, not the Earth, at the centre of the cosmos — the pivot of the Scientific Revolution, published as he lay dying.

name: Elizabeth I
description: Queen of England whose 45-year reign steadied a religiously divided realm, saw off the Spanish Armada (1588), and presided over a flowering of English drama and seafaring — while she mastered the politics of an unmarried female sovereign in a dynastic age.

name: Galileo Galilei
description: Pisan mathematician who turned the new telescope on the heavens — finding Jupiter's moons, Venus's phases, and lunar mountains — and championed Copernicanism until the Inquisition forced his abjuration. His kinematics laid groundwork for Newton.

name: Isaac Newton
description: English mathematician whose Principia (1687) unified terrestrial and celestial mechanics under three laws of motion and universal gravitation, and who co-invented calculus — establishing the mathematical framework of physics for two centuries.

name: Peter the Great
description: Russian tsar who dragged his realm toward European technology and administration — building a navy from nothing, defeating Sweden in the Great Northern War, and raising a new capital, Saint Petersburg, on the Baltic marshes.

name: Benjamin Franklin
description: Printer, scientist, and statesman: proved lightning electrical, invented the lightning rod and bifocals, edited the Declaration of Independence, and negotiated the French alliance and the peace that secured American independence.

name: Toussaint Louverture
description: Formerly enslaved general who led the Haitian Revolution — the only successful slave revolt to found a state — outmanoeuvring French, Spanish, and British armies before dying in a French prison a year before Haiti declared independence.

name: Napoleon Bonaparte
description: Corsican artillery officer who rode the French Revolution to emperor, redrew Europe's map through a decade of victories, and codified revolutionary law in the Code Napoléon — before Russia, Leipzig, and Waterloo ended the experiment at St Helena.

name: Simón Bolívar
description: Venezuelan general who liberated six South American nations from Spanish rule across campaigns of astonishing range, dreaming of a united Gran Colombia that fractured even before his death.

name: Charles Darwin
description: English naturalist whose voyage on HMS Beagle and twenty years of patient evidence-gathering produced On the Origin of Species (1859), establishing evolution by natural selection as the unifying principle of biology.

name: Abraham Lincoln
description: Sixteenth US president who preserved the Union through the Civil War, issued the Emancipation Proclamation, and pushed the Thirteenth Amendment abolishing slavery — assassinated days after victory.

name: Florence Nightingale
description: Founder of modern nursing whose sanitary reforms in Crimean War hospitals slashed death rates, and whose pioneering statistical graphics — the polar-area diagram — made mortality data politically undeniable.

name: Marie Curie
description: Polish-French physicist and chemist who coined 'radioactivity', discovered polonium and radium, and remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two sciences. Died of aplastic anaemia from radiation exposure.

name: Mahatma Gandhi
description: Leader of Indian independence whose satyagraha — mass nonviolent resistance, from the Salt March to Quit India — forced the end of the Raj and inspired civil-rights movements worldwide. Assassinated months after independence and Partition.

name: Albert Einstein
description: Physicist whose 1905 papers (special relativity, photoelectric effect, Brownian motion) and 1915 general relativity rebuilt the foundations of physics. A refugee from Nazi Germany, he became an icon of science and advocate for peace and civil rights.

name: Winston Churchill
description: British prime minister whose defiance and oratory rallied Britain through 1940's darkest months and helped forge the Allied coalition that defeated Nazi Germany. A polarizing imperialist elsewhere in his long career, he also won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
description: Only four-term US president: met the Great Depression with the New Deal's relief, recovery, and reform, then led America through World War II as chief architect of the Allied war effort and the postwar United Nations, governing from a wheelchair concealed from the public.

name: Alan Turing
description: Mathematician who defined computability with the Turing machine, led the Bletchley Park attack on the German Enigma cipher, and founded artificial-intelligence theory with the Turing test — before prosecution for homosexuality and early death. Pardoned 2013.

name: Nelson Mandela
description: Anti-apartheid revolutionary who emerged from 27 years in prison to negotiate the peaceful end of white-minority rule, win South Africa's first universal election in 1994, and pursue reconciliation through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

name: Martin Luther King Jr.
description: Baptist minister who led the American civil-rights movement through nonviolent mass action — Montgomery, Birmingham, the March on Washington and 'I Have a Dream' — winning the Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts before his assassination in Memphis.

name: Rosalind Franklin
description: X-ray crystallographer whose Photo 51 and analyses were decisive evidence for DNA's double helix, used without her knowledge by Watson and Crick. She later did foundational virus-structure work before dying at 37.

name: Yuri Gagarin
description: Soviet cosmonaut who became the first human in space aboard Vostok 1 on 12 April 1961, orbiting Earth once in 108 minutes and instantly becoming a global icon of the space age.
